It's a side of Monroe that the American public has rarely seen. "She hasn't really exploded as a star, yet she was on the brink of something big," says Dawnie Walton, deputy editor at Life.com, a Web site harboring more than 7 million Life magazine photographs. Last month, Walton stumbled upon the rare photographs while combing through the company's digital photo archives. Apparently, no one at Life.com even knew they were ever taken. I sent several rolls to Life in New York, but they wired back, 'Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?' In 1962, American photographer Bert Stern shot a tipsy, sometimes nude Monroe in a series of delicate shots that would be known as "The Last Sitting." Monroe died about six weeks later, on August 5, 1962. Life.com staff members say there are 15 million photographs in the Life archive dating back to the late 1850s, even before Life officially began publishing in 1936. Two years ago, the publication began slowly transferring the photographs into a digital archive. From time to time, unpublished photographs will be found that the company doesn't know existed. In April, Life.com released newly recovered, never-before-seen photographs of Martin Luther King Jr. taken by a Life photographer on the day King was assassinated at a Memphis, Tennessee, hotel in 1968.

(CNN) — The photographs were taken before Marilyn Monroe became known as the voluptuous blonde who radiated sex appeal in dozens of Hollywood films. They show a 24-year-old Monroe posing for *Life* magazine in August 1950—before rumors swirled about an affair with President John F. Kennedy, before her mental breakdowns became public, and before the beautiful actress died at age 36 from a mysterious overdose.

Discovered by Life.com last month, the collection of previously unpublished photographs reveals a softer, more innocent side of the budding 24-year-old starlet during a more peaceful period, before she reached the height of her fame. Her flawless face has a natural appearance, with minimal makeup—an unusual look for Monroe, who was often glamorized in photo shoots featuring lipstick, designer dresses and expensive jewelry.

Monday would have been Monroe’s 83rd birthday.

In one photograph, the young Monroe lies blissfully on a park bench, reading—a scene that Life.com editors believe was photographed at Griffith Park in Los Angeles, California. In another, she appears serene as she leans over a bridge, barefoot.

The 1950 photo shoot was conducted by *Life* photographer Ed Clark. It captures a side of Monroe that the American public has rarely seen.

“She hasn’t really exploded as a star, yet she was on the brink of something big,” said Dawnie Walton, deputy editor of Life.com, a website that houses more than 7 million *Life* magazine photographs. The site was launched in March. “I was amazed looking at her face. Although she looks very innocent, there is something very ... sexy.”

Walton discovered the rare images last month while searching through the company’s digital photo archives. Apparently, no one at Life.com even knew the photographs had been taken.

After investigating, Walton found that few notes had been left on the negatives. She believes the images were probably taken for a proposed cover shoot that was never used. Monroe did not appear on her first *Life* magazine cover until 1952.

*See some of the previously unpublished photographs of Monroe »*

“It just got lost and stowed away,” Walton said. “It was just ... somewhere in a warehouse in New Jersey.”

At the time of the shoot, Monroe had landed her first small breakout role, playing a mistress in “The Asphalt Jungle.” Although she had appeared in a handful of film cameos, she was still better known as a model.

Clark told the *Sarasota Herald-Tribune* that a friend at 20th Century Fox had alerted him that the studio had just signed “a hot tomato.”

“She was unknown then, so I was able to spend a lot of time shooting her,” Clark said. “We’d go out to Griffith Park and she’d read poetry. I sent several rolls to *Life* in New York, but they wired back, ‘Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?’”

Photographs taken later in the 1950s and early 1960s would portray a far more confident and sexual Monroe, producing images that became iconic in popular culture.

Among them is the famous 1955 photograph of a busty Monroe wearing a white halter dress as her skirt blows upward—a scene from her role in “The Seven Year Itch.” In 1962, American photographer Bert Stern captured a tipsy and sometimes nude Monroe in a series of delicate images that became known as “The Last Sitting.”

Monroe died about six weeks later, on August 5, 1962.

Life.com staff members say the *Life* archive contains 15 million photographs dating to the late 1850s—decades before the magazine officially began publishing in 1936. Two years ago, the publication began gradually transferring the photographs to a digital archive.

From time to time, staff members discover unpublished photographs whose existence was previously unknown to the company. In other cases, photographs were taken but never selected for publication.

Last March, to commemorate the 11th anniversary of Frank Sinatra’s death, Life.com released a series of unpublished photographs of the singer. In April, the site released newly recovered, never-before-seen photographs of Martin Luther King Jr., taken by a *Life* photographer at a Memphis, Tennessee, hotel on the day King was assassinated in 1968.

# Before the Icon: Marilyn Monroe in Griffith Park

In Ed Clark’s photographs, Marilyn Monroe does not yet look like a monument to herself.

She sits on the grass in Griffith Park wearing a simple sweater and trousers, her blond hair loose around her face. In some frames, she reads from a script; in others, she stretches out in the California sun or glances toward the camera with an expression that seems more curious than calculated. Los Angeles spreads beyond the park, but the city’s machinery of publicity feels momentarily distant.

The pictures were taken around 1950, when Monroe was still an aspiring actress rather than the most recognizable woman in Hollywood. Clark, a photographer for *LIFE*, reportedly went to photograph her after hearing from a contact at 20th Century Fox that the young performer was worth watching. The resulting images were not published by the magazine at the time—an irony that has become part of their history. Monroe was not yet famous enough to command the space.

That was about to change.

Born Norma Jeane Mortenson and raised amid foster homes and instability, Monroe entered the entertainment industry through modeling. Photographs came before major film roles: wartime factory images, pinup work and advertisements helped turn Norma Jeane into a camera-ready presence. She signed with 20th Century Fox in 1946, adopted the name Marilyn Monroe and began collecting small, often uncredited screen appearances. A brief contract at Columbia followed, along with more modeling and determined efforts to study acting.

By 1950, her career was beginning to gather momentum. Small but vivid parts in John Huston’s *The Asphalt Jungle* and Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s *All About Eve* showed that she could hold attention even when surrounded by established stars. She was not yet carrying films, but she had learned how to make a few minutes on screen feel consequential.

The Griffith Park session belongs to that transitional moment. Although often described as candid, the photographs came from an arranged shoot, and Monroe was already skilled at collaborating with a lens. Yet they retain an unusual informality. There are no diamonds, white fur or sculpted evening gowns. No subway grate sends a dress billowing around her legs. She is not playing the breathy, dazzled blonde who would later dominate films such as *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes*, *How to Marry a Millionaire* and *The Seven Year Itch*.

Instead, Clark’s camera finds a working actress between identities.

That distinction matters because Monroe’s later image was among the most carefully manufactured—and most relentlessly consumed—of the 20th century. Hollywood transformed her into a combination of innocence and sexual sophistication: platinum hair, red lips, clinging dresses, a soft voice and a smile that seemed both inviting and vulnerable. Monroe participated knowingly in that construction. She understood still photography with exceptional precision, changing her posture and expression almost imperceptibly to create the image a photographer needed.

But the persona became difficult to escape. Publicity reduced an ambitious, serious performer to “Marilyn,” a fantasy whose apparent spontaneity required discipline and repetition. Her struggles with studio control, typecasting, anxiety and insomnia rarely fit the cheerful image sold to audiences. Even her efforts to gain authority over her career—studying at the Actors Studio and forming Marilyn Monroe Productions—were often treated as surprising acts from someone the culture had decided not to take seriously.

Seen with hindsight, the Griffith Park pictures seem intimate because they precede that burden. Monroe appears young, hopeful and still available to possibility. The scripts in her hands are especially poignant. They suggest work rather than glamour: lines to learn, roles to win, a future not yet fixed.

It would be easy to call the photographs the “real” Marilyn and everything afterward a disguise. The truth is more complicated. Monroe was already performing for Clark, just as every portrait subject performs to some degree. The natural setting and casual clothes do not grant unfiltered access to Norma Jeane beneath the makeup.

What they offer instead is a record of scale. Here is Monroe before the image grew larger than the person—before every gesture became evidence for a public mythology of sex, sadness and doomed celebrity. The woman in Griffith Park is not yet frozen above a subway grate or encased in sequins beneath stage lights. She is simply an actress in Los Angeles, sitting in the grass with pages in her lap, waiting for Hollywood to learn her name.

## Forgotten Marilyn Monroe Photos Surface on What Would Have Been Her 83rd Birthday

**June 1, 2009** — Marilyn Monroe would have turned 83 today, and a newly unearthed collection of photographs is offering a rare glimpse of the screen legend before she became one of Hollywood’s most recognizable stars.

The images, taken by *Life* photographer Ed Clark in 1950, were discovered in the magazine’s digital archives after going unpublished for nearly six decades. They show a 24-year-old Monroe relaxing in Los Angeles’ Griffith Park, still on the verge of the fame that would follow films such as *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes*, *How to Marry a Millionaire* and *The Seven Year Itch*.

Life.com editor Dawnie Walton described the find as an exciting byproduct of exploring the publication’s vast photographic collection.

“We’re thrilled to be able to share these photos, which have basically been sitting in a warehouse for almost 60 years,” Walton said.

Clark photographed Monroe after a friend at 20th Century Fox suggested he meet the promising young actress. At the time, however, editors in New York apparently did not recognize her potential.

“I sent several rolls of film to *Life* in New York, but they wired back, ‘Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?’” Clark recalled.

The photographs capture a markedly different Monroe from the carefully styled blonde bombshell who would soon dominate movie screens and magazine covers. Dressed casually and photographed outdoors, she appears youthful, unguarded and far removed from the pressures of international celebrity.

Within a few years, Monroe would become a defining figure of 1950s Hollywood. Her life and career were cut short when she died in 1962 at age 36, but her image has remained an enduring part of popular culture.

The rediscovered Clark photographs add an intimate early chapter to that legacy: a portrait of Marilyn Monroe just before the rest of the world learned her name.

# Hidden in the Contact Sheets: LIFE’s Rediscovered Photographs of Marilyn Monroe, Frank Sinatra and Martin Luther King Jr.

Long before digital photography made nearly every frame instantly accessible, a magazine assignment could produce hundreds of negatives while only a handful of pictures reached the printed page. The rest—alternate compositions, informal portraits and entire unpublished sessions—were filed away in envelopes and boxes. In the vast archive created by *LIFE* magazine, those overlooked frames became a parallel visual history of the 20th century.

Life.com’s archival features have brought many of those photographs back into public view. Among the most striking are previously unpublished images of a 24-year-old Marilyn Monroe, made before she became one of Hollywood’s defining stars. Other recovered collections have revealed a young Frank Sinatra at the height of early “Sinatramania” and offered unusually intimate views of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. away from podiums and mass demonstrations.

Together, the collections show why archival photography matters: it can complicate familiar icons, restore the quieter moments surrounding historic events and reveal how little of a photographer’s original work readers once saw.

## Marilyn Monroe Before the Myth

In 1950, Marilyn Monroe was 24 years old and still years away from the films that would cement her celebrity. She had accumulated small screen appearances and studio contracts, but she was not yet the instantly recognizable figure of *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes*, *The Seven Year Itch* or *Some Like It Hot*.

That year, *LIFE* photographer Ed Clark photographed Monroe in Los Angeles, including an outdoor session in Griffith Park. Clark later recalled receiving a tip from a contact at 20th Century Fox who urged him to photograph the promising young actress. The pictures were sent to *LIFE*, but the magazine did not publish them at the time. According to the story that became attached to the session, editors in New York responded with a dismissive question: “Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?”

In retrospect, the line is almost too perfect. It captures both the uncertainty of fame and the limits of editorial foresight. The woman in Clark’s photographs would soon become one of the most photographed people on Earth, yet the pictures initially seemed to document someone of little national interest.

When the negatives and contact sheets resurfaced through the *LIFE* archive, their appeal rested partly on hindsight. Viewers know what Monroe was about to become. Every expression can therefore look prophetic: a smile suggests the warmth that later captivated movie audiences; a distant glance appears to anticipate the isolation associated with her life; an apparently effortless pose hints at her growing command of the camera.

But the images are most revealing when they are not treated as omens. They show a working actress near the beginning of her ascent rather than “Marilyn Monroe” as a finished cultural invention. She appears youthful, alert and less encased in the elaborate styling that later defined her public image. The atmosphere is comparatively relaxed. There is no subway grate, no diamond-filled musical number and no crowd of reporters. Instead, Clark photographed a young performer testing how she might present herself to a national picture magazine.

That distinction matters. Monroe’s later image was produced through the combined efforts of studio publicity departments, costume designers, makeup artists, directors and photographers—as well as through her own careful understanding of performance. Clark’s frames capture an earlier stage in that construction. Her charisma is evident, but the mythology is not yet complete.

## The Value of the Unselected Frame

The Monroe collection also illustrates how magazine photography once worked. A photographer rarely arrived with the expectation that every exposure would be printed. Editors chose images to fit a story, page design, deadline and available space. Even excellent photographs could be rejected because the subject was not considered important enough, because a planned article was canceled or because another news event displaced it.

Contact sheets preserved what publication erased. They recorded changes in posture and mood, experiments with angle and light, and transitions between formal poses. A single published portrait might present certainty; a sequence of adjacent frames could reveal hesitation, playfulness or collaboration between photographer and subject.

In Monroe’s case, the unpublished material challenges the impression that her image arrived fully formed. The sequence allows viewers to see variations rather than a single definitive icon. It is a record of becoming.

The rediscovery also changes the status of the photographs themselves. In 1950, they were pictures of a little-known actress that editors considered expendable. Decades later, they became rare documents of a global celebrity before fame transformed both her life and the way the public interpreted her face.

## Frank Sinatra and the Birth of a Modern Idol

Life.com has similarly revisited archival photographs of Frank Sinatra from the period when he emerged as a national sensation. In the early 1940s, Sinatra’s slender appearance, intimate singing style and appeal to teenage female fans made him a new kind of popular idol. The screaming “bobby-soxers” who crowded theaters and waited outside stage doors were not merely part of his story; they were evidence of a changing culture of celebrity.

Photographs preserved in the *LIFE* collection, including work associated with photographer John Florea, show both sides of that phenomenon. There is Sinatra the poised performer, carefully controlling a microphone and a room, and Sinatra the object of nearly overwhelming public attention. Images of fans—watching, shouting, reaching or waiting—are as important as portraits of the singer himself.

Seen as a group, the recovered or newly presented frames make clear that Sinatra’s fame was not only about music. It was about emotional identification, mass media and the emergence of youth audiences as a powerful cultural force. The photographs anticipate later scenes surrounding Elvis Presley, the Beatles and generations of pop stars.

They also preserve a Sinatra different from the later figure associated with Las Vegas, the Rat Pack and tuxedoed authority. Here he is young, narrow-shouldered and vulnerable-looking, a performer whose apparent sensitivity was central to his appeal. Like the Monroe photographs, the Sinatra archive captures a celebrity identity before it hardened into its most familiar form.

## Martin Luther King Jr. Beyond the Podium

The archival photographs involving Martin Luther King Jr. carry a different historical weight. King is most often remembered through a small set of monumental images: addressing the March on Washington, leading demonstrators, standing with fellow civil-rights leaders or confronting the machinery of segregation.

Those photographs remain indispensable, but they can flatten a life into a sequence of public symbols. Archival *LIFE* work—particularly intimate photographs by Grey Villet and other photojournalists who documented King, his family and the civil-rights movement—restores a more personal scale.

In these collections, King can appear not only as an orator or strategist but also as a husband, father, minister and exhausted human being. Photographs made in homes, churches, offices and quieter moments between public events disclose the emotional and practical burden carried by King and those around him. Coretta Scott King and the couple’s children cease to be background figures and become part of the historical narrative.

Such images do not diminish King’s stature. Instead, they clarify the cost of his public role. The civil-rights movement depended on speeches and marches, but it was also lived through telephone calls, family separations, security fears, planning meetings, travel and constant pressure. Informal photographs can communicate those realities with a directness that ceremonial images cannot.

They also remind viewers that the movement was composed of individuals rather than abstractions. A photograph of King resting, speaking privately or interacting with his family creates a different relationship with history than an image of him before a vast crowd. One shows the public leader; the other helps reveal the person required to sustain that leadership.

## Three Kinds of American Fame

Placed beside one another, the Monroe, Sinatra and King collections trace three very different forms of 20th-century visibility.

Monroe represents cinematic celebrity and the creation of a visual persona. Sinatra embodies mass fandom, recorded music and the rise of the modern pop idol. King represents moral and political leadership under the relentless scrutiny of the news media.

All three understood, in different ways, the power of the camera. Monroe could transform herself in its presence. Sinatra used performance and apparent intimacy to reach listeners far beyond the stage. King recognized that photographs of disciplined protest and racist violence could move national opinion.

Yet the archival pictures are often most compelling when those public roles loosen. Monroe is not yet sealed inside the image of “Marilyn.” Sinatra is not yet the commanding elder statesman of popular entertainment. King is not only the monumental figure of commemorative history. The unpublished photographs return uncertainty, youth, fatigue and spontaneity to people later turned into symbols.

## The Archive as an Unfinished History

Life.com’s archival discoveries are more than exercises in nostalgia. They demonstrate that a photographic archive is not a neutral storehouse. It contains both what editors considered important and what they overlooked. Revisiting it can expose earlier judgments, recover neglected work and alter the visual record inherited by later generations.

The unseen Monroe photographs are the clearest example of editorial uncertainty becoming historical irony. Images once passed over because the subject was insufficiently famous are now valuable precisely because they show her before fame. The Sinatra photographs expand the story from a star’s portrait to the social phenomenon surrounding him. The King collections bring private strain and family life into a history often dominated by public triumph and tragedy.

Archives do not literally reveal the past untouched. Every rediscovery involves new choices: which negatives to scan, how to sequence them, what captions to write and what context to provide. Nevertheless, the recovery of unpublished photographs widens the field of evidence. It allows viewers to look beyond the few frames that originally defined an event or person.

That is the enduring fascination of *LIFE*’s hidden contact sheets. They preserve moments that editors could not yet recognize as historic—and faces that history had not finished transforming into icons.
